title: Select K Disjoint Special Substrings
statement:
You are given a string `s` of lowercase English letters and an integer `k`. A non-empty substring of `s` is **special** when both of these hold:

- every letter that occurs in the substring has all of its occurrences in `s` inside the substring, and
- the substring is not the whole of `s`.

Return `true` if you can pick `k` special substrings of which no two overlap (share a position of `s`), and `false` otherwise. Picking zero substrings is always possible.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Testing all O(n²) substrings is slow. A special substring must begin at the **first occurrence** of its first letter, so there are at most 26 possible starts. From `first[c]`, stretch the end to the last occurrence of every letter met; if a letter met also occurs before the start, no special substring starts there. Any special substring contains the smallest one with the same start, so swapping chosen substrings for these smallest ones keeps them disjoint. That leaves at most 26 candidate intervals (dropping one that is all of `s`), and the question becomes interval scheduling: sort by right end and pick every interval that starts after the last pick.

## Approach

1. Record `first` and `last`, each letter's first and last index.
2. For each letter `c` present, set `start = first[c]`, `end = last[c]` and scan `i` from `start` to `end`. If the letter at `i` first appears before `start`, the start is invalid; otherwise stretch `end` to that letter's last index.
3. If the scan stays valid and `[start, end]` is not all of `s`, add it to `intervals`.
4. Sort `intervals` by end and pick each one that starts after `prevEnd`, counting picks in `count`.
5. Return `count >= k`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abcdbaefab"`, `k = 2`. `a` spans 0 to 8 and `b` spans 1 to 9; `c`, `d`, `e` and `f` occur once, at 2, 3, 6 and 7.

- `a`: the scan meets `b` and stretches `end` to 9; `[0, 9]` is all of `s`, so it is dropped.
- `b`: from 1, the scan reaches `a` at index 5, whose first copy is at 0, so this start is invalid.
- `c`, `d`, `e`, `f` give `[2, 2]`, `[3, 3]`, `[6, 6]` and `[7, 7]`.

None of these overlap, so `count = 4`, and `4 >= 2` gives `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(26 · n): each of at most 26 scans crosses the string at most once; sorting 26 intervals costs a constant.
- Space: O(26) for the letter tables and the intervals.

## Pitfalls

- The whole string never counts: `"abcabc"` has no special substring, so `k = 1` gives `false`.
- `end` grows during the scan; the loop condition must read the updated value, or letters near the new end are never checked.
- Prefer short intervals: for `"xabxq"`, `[0, 3]` (from `x`) is special, but picking it blocks `a` and `b`. Sorting by end picks `a`, `b` and `q`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `first`, `last` | first and last index of each letter, -1 when absent |
| `c` | letter whose first occurrence is the candidate start |
| `start`, `end` | the candidate interval; `end` grows during the scan |
| `valid` | no scanned letter has a copy before `start` |
| `i`, `ch` | scan position and its letter |
| `intervals` | the smallest special substrings, as `[start, end]` |
| `count`, `prevEnd` | intervals picked so far, and where the last pick ends |
